claim: Linear array electrodes have become a ubiquitous electrophysiological tool for understanding the functional roles of neural populations across the layers of the cortex.
source: Linear array electrodes have become a ubiquitous electrophysiological tool for understanding the functional roles of neural populations across the layers of the cortex, their interactions, and the computations they perform.
evidence: This is a statement about the widespread use of linear array electrodes in neuroscience research, drawing from established scientific practice.

claim: The gold standard for identifying laminar compartments from functional recordings is current-source density (CSD) analysis.
source: The gold standard for identifying laminar compartments from functional recordings is current-source density (CSD) analysis (Mitzdorf, 1985; Mitzdorf and Singer, 1978; Schroeder et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work establishing CSD as the standard method.

claim: The CSD represents the second spatial derivative of local field potential (LFP) activity averaged to repeated events.
source: The CSD represents the second spatial derivative of local field potential (LFP) activity averaged to repeated events.
evidence: This is a definition of CSD based on established methodology in the field.

claim: Sensory-evoked stimulation produces feedforward activation of the canonical cortical columnar circuit via activation of the input layer.
source: These events are often sensory-evoked stimulation as in flashed visual stimuli in visual cortex (Maier et al., 2010; Schroeder et al., 1991; Wang et al., 2020) or short duration sounds in auditory cortex (Happel et al., 2010; Lakatos et al., 2007; Szymanski et al., 2011) which produce feedforward activation of the canonical cortical columnar circuit via activation of the input layer (Gratiy et al., 2011; Mitzdorf, 1985; Mitzdorf and Singer, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The earliest current sink in CSD reflects the feedforward activation of the input layers.
source: The earliest current sink reflects the feedforward activation of the input layers (Mitzdorf, 1987; Mitzdorf, 1985), and the current sources above and below are used to estimate the boundaries with respect to superficial (layers 1–3) and deep (layers 5 and 6) cortical layers (Self et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CSD analysis has been validated histologically.
source: CSD analysis has been validated histologically (Mitzdorf and Singer, 1979; Schroeder et al., 1991; Takeuchi et al., 2011) and reliably captures known laminar differences in the functional properties of cortical layers, such as differences in evoked latencies across layers in response to driving input (Bode-Greuel et al., 1987; Einevoll et al., 2013; Plomp et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous histological validation studies.

claim: CSD analysis has largely been limited to primary sensory areas where the types of sensory stimuli that can robustly and reliably generate the evoked responses necessary for averaging CSDs are well established.
source: CSD analysis has largely been limited to primary sensory areas where the types of sensory stimuli that can robustly and reliably generate the evoked responses necessary for averaging CSDs are well established.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CSD analysis based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: CSD analysis has been used in higher-order cortical areas where sensory-evoked responses are apparent, such as visual responses in frontal cortex.
source: Although CSD analysis has been used in higher-order cortical areas where sensory-evoked responses are apparent, such as visual responses in frontal cortex (Bastos et al., 2018; Godlove et al., 2014), it is less clear what to use as a triggering event in non-sensory cortical areas to reveal similar laminar patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ongoing spiking activity is strongly coupled to the phase of LFP fluctuations in the cortex.
source: Previous work has shown ongoing spiking activity is strongly coupled to the phase of LFP fluctuations in the cortex (Davis et al., 2022; Destexhe et al., 1999; Dotson et al., 2014; Eeckman and Freeman, 1990; Esghaei et al., 2018; Haegens et al., 2011) and these spike–field relationships can be diagnostic of circuit interactions in cortical systems (Safavi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Spike-field relationships can be diagnostic of circuit interactions in cortical systems.
source: Previous work has shown ongoing spiking activity is strongly coupled to the phase of LFP fluctuations in the cortex (Davis et al., 2022; Destexhe et al., 1999; Dotson et al., 2014; Eeckman and Freeman, 1990; Esghaei et al., 2018; Haegens et al., 2011) and these spike–field relationships can be diagnostic of circuit interactions in cortical systems (Safavi et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There is a phase reversal in spike-field coupling that reliably corresponds to the laminar boundary between input and deep layers as estimated by CSD.
source: We find that there is a phase reversal in spike–field coupling that reliably corresponds to the laminar boundary between input and deep layers as estimated by CSD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The phase reversal pattern reliably reversed in awake recordings from both common marmosets and rhesus macaque in multiple cortical areas including extrastriate visual and prefrontal cortex.
source: This pattern reliably reversed in awake recordings from both common marmosets and rhesus macaque in multiple cortical areas including extrastriate visual and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from multiple species and cortical areas presented in the manuscript.

claim: Electrophysiology data were recorded from 32-channel linear probes inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface into cortical regions V4 in two macaque monkeys and middle temporal (MT) or pre-frontal cortex (PFC) in two marmoset monkeys.
source: We recorded electrophysiology data from 32-channel linear probes (Atlas Neuroengineering) inserted perpendicular to the cortical surface into cortical regions V4 in two macaque monkeys and middle temporal (MT) or pre-frontal cortex (PFC) in two marmoset monkeys performing head-fixed visual tasks under various experimental conditions (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The superficial channels had an average SPI value of 0.162 ± 0.012.
source: The superficial channels had an average SPI value of 0.162 ± 0.012 (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM]; N = 34 sessions; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: The superficial layer SPI was significantly greater than the input layer SPI (0.122 ± 0.010).
source: This was significantly greater than the input layer (SPI = 0.122 ± 0.010 mean ± SEM; p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 2c), and both were significantly greater than the deep layers (SPI = 0.073 ± 0.009 SEM; p = 0.000003 S. v. D. and p = 0.000009 I. v. D.; Figure 2d, e).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measurements from the data.

claim: Both superficial and input layer SPI were significantly greater than the deep layer SPI (0.073 ± 0.009).
source: This was significantly greater than the input layer (SPI = 0.122 ± 0.010 mean ± SEM; p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 2c), and both were significantly greater than the deep layers (SPI = 0.073 ± 0.009 SEM; p = 0.000003 S. v. D. and p = 0.000009 I. v. D.; Figure 2d, e).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measurements from the data.

claim: The preferred LFP phase angle for spiking in the superficial and input layers was 2.86 and −2.68 rad, respectively, which corresponds toward the trough of ongoing LFP fluctuations.
source: The preferred LFP phase angle (i.e. the circular mean of the phase distribution) for spiking in the superficial and input layers was 2.86 and −2.68 rad, respectively, which corresponds toward the trough of ongoing LFP fluctuations.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data analysis.

claim: The preferred phase angle for deep layer spiking (−1.44 rad) was significantly different from the preferred phase angle for superficial and input layer spiking.
source: This was significantly different from the preferred phase angle for deep layer spiking (−1.44 rad; F = 38.52, p < 1 × 10−7 and F = 21.15, p = 0.00002, respectively; Watson–Williams test; Figure 2f) suggesting that indeed the deeper layers may be distinguished by a change in the preferred spike–LFP phase angle relative to the superficial electrodes and this could be read out from the spike–LFP relationship across the depth of the cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measurements from the data.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the depth of the bottom of the input layer estimated from CSD analysis and the depth of the phase reversal (r = 0.64, p = 0.00005).
source: There was a significant correlation between the depth estimated from the CSD and the phase reversal (r = 0.64, p = 0.00005; Pearson's correlation) and no significant difference between the estimated depth values (mean difference = 271 ± 49 μm SEM; p = 0.98, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing two methods of depth estimation.

claim: There was no significant difference between the estimated depth values from CSD and phase reversal (mean difference = 271 ± 49 μm SEM; p = 0.98).
source: There was a significant correlation between the depth estimated from the CSD and the phase reversal (r = 0.64, p = 0.00005; Pearson's correlation) and no significant difference between the estimated depth values (mean difference = 271 ± 49 μm SEM; p = 0.98, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of measurements from the data.

claim: The observed phase reversal was apparent in multiple frequency bands (4–8, 8–14, 15–30, and 30–50 Hz).
source: To test this we filtered the data in a variety of commonly used frequency bands (4–8, 8–14, 15–30, and 30–50 Hz) and calculated phase using the Hilbert Transform (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). We found that the observed phase reversal was apparent in each case, indicating the results were not dependent on the filter or the method used to compute phase.
evidence: This describes testing the robustness of the finding across different analysis parameters.

claim: The results were not dependent on the filter or the method used to compute phase.
source: We found that the observed phase reversal was apparent in each case, indicating the results were not dependent on the filter or the method used to compute phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from testing multiple analysis parameters.

claim: The same relationship between laminar depth and preferred phase angle was observed when using single-unit spiking activity as when using multi-unit spiking activity.
source: We performed the same analysis aligning cross-channel LPC from single units across recording sessions based on CSD depth (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). We observed the same relationship between laminar depth and preferred phase angle as when using multi-unit spiking activity.
evidence: This describes testing the robustness of the finding using different spike sorting approaches.

claim: The cross-channel LPC revealed qualitatively similar depths for the laminar-phase reversal across experimental conditions within the same penetration.
source: We also separated out different conditions during the same recording session where the electrode placement was unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). These included fixation during a visual task, freely viewing natural scene images, freely viewing in total darkness, and fixation during receptive field mapping. The cross-channel LPC revealed qualitatively similar depths for the laminar-phase reversal across experimental conditions within the same penetration.
evidence: This describes testing the robustness of the finding across different behavioral conditions.

claim: The phase reversal persisted under all referencing conditions tested (shallowest contact, deepest contact, or common average reference).
source: In order to test whether our results depended on the location of the reference contact we re-referenced the LFP data to the shallowest contact, the deepest contact, or a common average reference (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The phase reversal persisted under all referencing conditions.
evidence: This describes testing the robustness of the finding across different referencing schemes.

claim: As little as a minute of continuously recorded data is sufficient to recover the phase reversal across channels.
source: Further, as little as a minute of continuously recorded data is sufficient to recover the phase reversal across channels.
evidence: This is a statement about the minimum data requirements for the method.

claim: The depth of the phase reversal moved over the course of 15 min in an example recording session.
source: To demonstrate this, we calculated LPC on sequential 3-min epochs during the first 15 min of an example recording session (Figure 3—figure supplement 6). We found the depth of the phase reversal moved over the course of 15 min.
evidence: This describes an observation from tracking the phase reversal over time.

claim: There was a significant difference in the estimated depth of the input layer from the spike-phase reversal between the first and last 2 min across all recordings (p = 0.005).
source: When comparing the depth after the first or last 2 min across all recordings, we found a significant difference in the estimated depth of the input layer from the spike-phase reversal (p = 0.005, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) such that the estimate of input layer depth consistently drifted deeper across recording sessions by an average of 132 ± 26 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of depth changes over time.

claim: The estimate of input layer depth consistently drifted deeper across recording sessions by an average of 132 ± 26 μm.
source: When comparing the depth after the first or last 2 min across all recordings, we found a significant difference in the estimated depth of the input layer from the spike-phase reversal (p = 0.005, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) such that the estimate of input layer depth consistently drifted deeper across recording sessions by an average of 132 ± 26 μm (SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of electrode drift.

claim: This change in the depth estimate across the recording is consistent with electrode drift from movement of the probe relative to the cortex as the tissue settles at the start of the recording.
source: This change in the depth estimate across the recording is consistent with electrode drift from movement of the probe relative to the cortex as the tissue settles at the start of the recording.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed depth changes over time.

claim: On many recording sessions a characteristic phase correlation pattern was found that seemed to align well with both CSD and LPC depth estimates.
source: On many recording sessions we found a characteristic phase correlation pattern that seemed to align well with both CSD and LPC depth estimates (Figure 4a–c), and across many recordings the phase correlations within layers could dissociate laminar compartments.
evidence: This describes an observation from analyzing LFP phase correlations.

claim: Some sessions yielded phase correlation patterns that were noisy and difficult to interpret.
source: However, this was not always the case. Some sessions yielded phase correlation patterns that were noisy and difficult to interpret, although knowing where the boundary was made it easier to identify the characteristic pattern (Figure 4d, e).
evidence: This describes variability in the reliability of LFP phase correlations.

claim: The spike–LFP phase relationship appears to provide a more robust measure of contact depth than LFP phase correlations alone.
source: While, on average, LFP phase correlations can be informative (Figure 4f), the spike–LFP phase relationship appears to provide a more robust measure of contact depth.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment of two methods based on the data.

claim: There were 14 out of 34 instances where there was 200 μm or more disagreement between CSD and LPC estimates for the location of the input layer.
source: Across our recordings there were some instances (14/34) where there was 200 μm or more disagreement between CSD and LPC estimates for the location of the input layer relative to the probe contacts.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of disagreement between methods.

claim: Previous work in multiple cortical areas has shown that the superficial layers have lower firing rates as compared to the input and deep layers.
source: First, previous work in multiple cortical areas has shown that the superficial layers have lower firing rates as compared to the input and deep layers (de Kock and Sakmann, 2009; Haegens et al., 2015; Lakatos et al., 2005; Leszczyński et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: On sessions where CSD and LPC estimates differed by more than 200 μm, the CSD aligned firing rates failed to recapitulate the finding of higher firing rates in the input and deeper layers (p = 0.09).
source: We found that on these sessions, the CSD aligned firing rates failed to recapitulate the finding of higher firing rates in the input and deeper layers (p = 0.09, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing firing rates aligned to CSD estimates.

claim: When aligned to the LPC estimate, significantly stronger input firing rates were found (p = 0.0003).
source: Conversely, we did find significantly stronger input firing rates when aligned to the LPC estimate (p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), suggesting the LPC estimate on these sessions was better aligned than the CSD to the ground truth.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing firing rates aligned to LPC estimates.

claim: The LPC estimate on sessions with disagreement was better aligned than the CSD to the ground truth.
source: Conversely, we did find significantly stronger input firing rates when aligned to the LPC estimate (p = 0.0003, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), suggesting the LPC estimate on these sessions was better aligned than the CSD to the ground truth.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the firing rate analysis.

claim: Previous groups have reported an inversion in the spectral content of the LFP across layers, with the superficial layers exhibiting more high-frequency power (e.g. 80–200 Hz) and the deep layers exhibiting more low-frequency power (8–20 Hz).
source: We next examined a second previously reported finding that varied with laminar depth. Previous groups have reported an inversion in the spectral content of the LFP across layers, with the superficial layers exhibiting more high-frequency power (e.g. 80–200 Hz) and the deep layers exhibiting more low-frequency power (8–20 Hz) (Maier et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The crossover between the power in higher and lower frequencies was reported to occur around the input layers defined from CSD measurements.
source: The crossover between the power in higher and lower frequencies was reported to occur around the input layers defined from CSD measurements (Bastos et al., 2018), and validated histologically in multiple cortical areas (Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The depth estimate from the LPC measure was significantly correlated with the high/low power inversion (Pearson's r = 0.87, p = 0.00005).
source: The depth estimate from the LPC measure was significantly correlated with the high/low power inversion (Pearson's r = 0.87, p = 0.00005) whereas the CSD estimate was more weakly, although still significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.65, p = 0.012), indicating that on the recording sessions where there was some disparity between the CSD and LPC estimate (Figure 6d), the LPC better captured the power inversion than the CSD measure (Figure 6e, f).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing depth estimates to LFP power patterns.

claim: The CSD estimate was more weakly, although still significantly correlated with the high/low power inversion (Pearson's r = 0.65, p = 0.012).
source: The depth estimate from the LPC measure was significantly correlated with the high/low power inversion (Pearson's r = 0.87, p = 0.00005) whereas the CSD estimate was more weakly, although still significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.65, p = 0.012), indicating that on the recording sessions where there was some disparity between the CSD and LPC estimate (Figure 6d), the LPC better captured the power inversion than the CSD measure (Figure 6e, f).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing depth estimates to LFP power patterns.

claim: On recording sessions where there was disparity between the CSD and LPC estimate, the LPC better captured the power inversion than the CSD measure.
source: The depth estimate from the LPC measure was significantly correlated with the high/low power inversion (Pearson's r = 0.87, p = 0.00005) whereas the CSD estimate was more weakly, although still significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.65, p = 0.012), indicating that on the recording sessions where there was some disparity between the CSD and LPC estimate (Figure 6d), the LPC better captured the power inversion than the CSD measure (Figure 6e, f).
evidence: This is a comparative assessment based on statistical analysis.

claim: When noise or error in assigning laminar compartments based on CSD analysis occur, the LPC phase reversal is a more reliable measure of laminar depth.
source: These results suggest that when noise or error in assigning laminar compartments based on CSD analysis occur, the LPC phase reversal is a more reliable measure of laminar depth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analyses of CSD and LPC.

claim: CSD analysis requires averaging across repeated discrete sensory events that may be difficult to generate in less well-studied cortical areas where the response selectivity is not apparent.
source: However, CSD analysis requires averaging across repeated discrete sensory events that may be difficult to generate in less well-studied cortical areas where the response selectivity is not apparent.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of CSD analysis based on methodological requirements.

claim: CSDs can be calculated from intrinsic events such as up/down state transitions or bursts of oscillatory power.
source: While CSDs can also be calculated from intrinsic events such as up/down state transitions (Senzai et al., 2019) or bursts of oscillatory power (Bollimunta et al., 2008), it is less clear how reliable their patterns reflect the laminar organization of the underlying circuitry with respect to distinct anatomical boundaries – although methods have been proposed to recover spatial information from spontaneous activity (Chand and Dhamala, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Using LPC to identify laminar compartments, the pattern of LFP power reversing across the input layer observed in multiple cortical areas and validated histologically was replicated.
source: Using LPC to identify laminar compartments, we are able to replicate the pattern of LFP power reversing across the input layer observed in multiple cortical areas and has been validated histologically (Bastos et al., 2018; Maier et al., 2010; Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes replicating a previously validated finding using the new method.

claim: The LPC measurement is more reliable in epochs in which thousands of spikes have occurred compared to hundreds of spikes.
source: While the number of spikes necessary to recover the spike-phase inversion can be counted in the hundreds, the LPC measurement is more reliable in epochs in which thousands of spikes have occurred.
evidence: This is a statement about the data requirements for reliable LPC measurements.

claim: There are occasions where correlations in LFP phase are sufficient to provide strong evidence of the location of laminar boundaries.
source: It would be convenient if LFP phase alone were sufficient to identify cortical layers as this would eliminate the requirement for measuring multi-unit spiking on multiple electrodes, and indeed we find there are occasions where correlations in LFP phase are sufficient to provide strong evidence of the location of laminar boundaries.
evidence: This describes observations about the utility of LFP phase correlations.

claim: The reliability of the pattern of LFP phase correlation varies across the recordings in the dataset.
source: However, we find the reliability of this pattern of LFP phase correlation varies across the recordings in our dataset, although the reason why is unclear.
evidence: This describes variability in the reliability of LFP phase correlations.

claim: Measures of cortical depth are improved when LFP phase is combined with the preferred timing of spiking activity across the cortical layers.
source: We do find measures of cortical depth are improved when LFP phase is combined with the preferred timing of spiking activity across the cortical layers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different analysis approaches.

claim: The superficial and input layers of cortex show stronger spike–LFP coupling than the deeper layers.
source: One interesting observation is that the superficial and input layers of cortex show stronger spike–LFP coupling than the deeper layers.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The LFP may be largely reflecting the shared synaptic inputs in the numerous connections in the superficial and input cortical layers.
source: It may be that the LFP is largely reflecting the shared synaptic inputs in the numerous connections in these cortical layers (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern, supported by a citation.

claim: Spike-count correlations were observed to be stronger in the superficial and input layers and weaker in the deep layers in V2.
source: This is consistent with measurements of correlated variability in V2 where spike-count correlations were observed to be stronger in the superficial and input layers and weaker in the deep layers (Smith et al., 2013), or in V4 where the strongest correlations were observed in the input layers relative to the superficial or deep layers (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In V4, the strongest correlations were observed in the input layers relative to the superficial or deep layers.
source: This is consistent with measurements of correlated variability in V2 where spike-count correlations were observed to be stronger in the superficial and input layers and weaker in the deep layers (Smith et al., 2013), or in V4 where the strongest correlations were observed in the input layers relative to the superficial or deep layers (Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In V1, the superficial and deep layers showed stronger spike-count correlations and the input layers showed weaker correlations.
source: A different pattern has been observed in V1, where the superficial and deep layers showed stronger spike-count correlations and in the input layers showed weaker correlations (Hansen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: One might predict that a different pattern of spike-phase coupling would occur in V1.
source: One might predict that a different pattern of spike-phase coupling would occur in V1, although the contribution of an anesthetized state is unclear.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on previous findings in V1.

claim: Reliable patterns were found across V4, MT, and PFC, and across two species of monkey performing visually guided tasks.
source: We find reliable patterns across V4, MT, and PFC, and across two species of monkey performing visually guided tasks.
evidence: This summarizes the generalizability of the findings across areas and species.

claim: It is not yet known if the same observations hold in cortical areas with non-sensory responses, under conditions of sleep or anesthesia, or in other species.
source: Our findings may be limited to these conditions, as we do not yet know if the same observations hold in cortical areas with non-sensory responses, under conditions of sleep or anesthesia, or in other species.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and unknowns about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The predominantly radial architecture of cortical fibers between superficial and deep layers may form an electrical dipole that spans across the layers of the cortex.
source: One possibility stems from the hypothesis that the predominantly radial architecture of cortical fibers between superficial and deep layers forms an electrical dipole that spans across the layers of the cortex (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the mechanism underlying the observed pattern, supported by a citation.

claim: The observed spike-phase reversal may occur due to the sources of LFP phase inverting across a dipole generated by the structure of the parallel radial processes of pyramidal cells that arborize in the superficial layers.
source: The prediction, therefore, is that the observed spike-phase reversal occurs due to the sources of LFP phase inverting across a dipole generated by the structure of the parallel radial processes of pyramidal cells that arborize in the superficial layers (however see Riera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the mechanism, with a citation noting alternative views.

claim: The reversal is well aligned to the boundary that separates the input and deep layers in multiple cortical areas.
source: While the network mechanism responsible for the observed phase reversal remains unclear, our results indicate the reversal is well aligned to the boundary that separates the input and deep layers in multiple cortical areas.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding across cortical areas.

claim: The LPC method could be a useful supplement to CSD analysis as it provides a source of cross-validation for potentially noisy or ambiguous CSD patterns.
source: The LPC method for estimating laminar depth described here could be a useful supplement to CSD analysis as it provides a source of cross-validation for potentially noisy or ambiguous CSD patterns.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the method based on the findings.

claim: LPC is fast and simple, making it well suited to online depth estimation from unsorted multi-unit spiking activity.
source: The advantages of the LPC method are that it is fast and simple, making it well suited to online depth estimation from unsorted multi-unit spiking activity.
evidence: This describes practical advantages of the method.

claim: LPC can be estimated from ongoing activity in a variety of experimental conditions, cortical areas, and analysis parameters.
source: LPC can be estimated from ongoing activity in a variety of experimental conditions, cortical areas, and analysis parameters, and may help relate the function of neural populations to the fundamental computation of information processing in the columnar cortical circuit.
evidence: This summarizes the robustness and potential utility of the method.

claim: Data from two adult male marmoset monkeys (2 and 3 years of age) and two adult male rhesus macaques (13 and 15 years of age) were used in this study.
source: Data from two adult male marmoset monkeys (2 and 3 years of age; Callithrix jacchus) and two adult male rhesus macaques (13 and 15 years of age; Macaca mulatta) were used in this study.
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Data from the macaques were previously published in Franken and Reynolds, 2021.
source: Data from the macaques were previously published in Franken and Reynolds, 2021.
evidence: This indicates that some data were from a previous publication.

claim: All surgical procedures were performed with the monkeys under general anesthesia in an aseptic environment in accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
source: All surgical procedures were performed with the monkeys under general anesthesia in an aseptic environment in accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This describes the ethical standards followed in the study.

claim: All experimental methods were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Salk Institute for Biological Studies and conformed with NIH guidelines (protocol 14-00014).
source: All experimental methods were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Salk Institute for Biological Studies and conformed with NIH guidelines (protocol 14-00014).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Electrode voltages were recorded from a 32-channel linear silicone electrode array connected to an Intan RHD2000 USB interface board.
source: Electrode voltages were recorded from a 32-channel linear silicone electrode array (Atlas Neuroengineering; Leuven, Belgium) connected to an Intan RHD2000 USB interface board (Intan Technologies LLC, Los Angeles, USA) controlled by a Windows computer.
evidence: This describes the recording equipment used.

claim: Data were sampled at 30 kHz from all channels.
source: Data were sampled at 30 kHz from all channels.
evidence: This describes the sampling rate used for data acquisition.

claim: Spike data were high-pass filtered at 500 Hz and candidate spike waveforms were defined as exceeding 4 standard deviations of a sliding 1-s window of ongoing voltage fluctuations.
source: Spike data were high-pass filtered at 500 Hz and candidate spike waveforms were defined as exceeding 4 standard deviations of a sliding 1-s window of ongoing voltage fluctuations.
evidence: This describes the spike detection methodology.

claim: LFP data were low-pass filtered at 300 Hz and down-sampled to 1000 Hz.
source: LFP data were low-pass filtered at 300 Hz and down-sampled to 1000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the LFP processing methodology.

claim: Sessions were only included if CSD analysis revealed a recognizable source–sink pattern consistent with reversals across superficial and deep layers.
source: Sessions were only included if CSD analysis revealed a recognizable source–sink pattern consistent with reversals across superficial and deep layers.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for recording sessions.

claim: Six recording sessions from V4 in each macaque, 8 recording sessions in marmoset MT, and 14 recording sessions from marmoset PFC were used in the analyses across recordings.
source: Six recording sessions from V4 in each macaque, 8 recording sessions in marmoset MT, and 14 recording sessions from marmoset PFC were used in the analyses across recordings.
evidence: This describes the sample sizes for different cortical areas.
